title: Radiolarian species lack definite geographic ranges and many co-occur locally

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Radiolarian species lack definite geographic ranges and many co-occur locally

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Radiolarian species show vague distributions in space and time: many occur worldwide without specific geographic limits, families and genera appear unchanged since the Cambrian, and a small sample of sediment typically contains scores or hundreds of forms with no local predominance of one species.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the distribution of species in space is curious and vague; many species are found all over the world, or at least every here and there, with no evidence of specific limitations of geographical habitat

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter IX, “On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons”; topic “Radiolarian species and distribution”. Scope: Radiolaria, living and fossil

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch09-12: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.74

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Distribution and assemblage claims map directly to occurrence records, and large open databases exist. Biases and incomplete identification weaken global and Cambrian-era conclusions, but major parts are presently testable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate species range sizes, occupancy, local richness, dominance and fossil first occurrences from georeferenced living and fossil records, with standardized sampling and taxonomic validation. The claim predicts unusually broad ranges, high local richness, weak dominance and long genus or family durations.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Sampling effort is highly uneven in space, depth and geological time.

Micropaleontological taxonomy has substantial synonymy and revision.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Range, dominance and first appearance are standard occurrence statistics, and radiolarians are present in open marine and fossil databases that a small team can query directly. Coverage is uneven between living plankton, deep-sea cores and Paleozoic rocks, but it is enough to confirm or refute worldwide ranges, local diversity and the Cambrian claim. Effort bias is real and is handled by rarefaction rather than by collecting new samples.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: From occurrence tables, measure geographic range sizes, sample-level richness and evenness, and the stratigraphic span of families and genera, including whether living taxa are already present in the Cambrian. Cosmopolitan ranges, high local richness without single-species dominance, and Cambrian-to-Recent identity would support the claim; endemic ranges, dominance, or much later first appearances would refute the corresponding clause.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Deep-sea drilling archives are strongest in the Cenozoic, so Paleozoic coverage depends on other occurrence compilations.

Sampling effort and taxonomic lumping can mimic cosmopolitanism and high local richness.
